## Web Searcher: emerging 2025-2026 style movements and the anti-generic discourse

Research question: "Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules."

Your angle: **emerging 2025-2026 style movements and the anti-generic discourse** — Area 3, and the pipeline's anti-template core rule. Needs current practitioner writing (Codrops, Awwwards, Rauno Freiberg, Emil Kowalski, design-press critique) to name both what is newly legible as a movement with its own failure mode, and what has calcified into the Tailwind/AI-default cliché the pipeline must explicitly avoid.
Search query: `named web design aesthetic movements 2026 beyond brutalism and glassmorphism — anti-design, spatial and Liquid Glass, editorial revival, dimensional type — and critique of the AI-default templated homogenized website look`

## Task
Use WebSearch with the query above (or a refined version). Return the top 4-6 most relevant results.
Rank by relevance to the ORIGINAL question, not just the search query. Skip obvious SEO spam/content farms.
Include a short snippet capturing why each result is relevant.

Structured output only.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

- _gstack-command: Router for the gstack skill suite. (gstack)
- academic-paper-composer: Systematic writing framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers from optimized outline to submission-ready manuscript. Use when users want to: (1) write a paper from a detailed outline, (2) ensure quality control during writing, (3) maintain consistency across chapters, (4) prepare a submission-ready manuscript, or (5) systematically execute a planned paper. Triggered by phrases like 'write the paper from this outline,' 'compose the full manuscript,' 'execute the outline,' or when users have completed strategic planning (academic-paper-strategist skill) and are ready to write. Takes optimized outline as input; outputs complete manuscript with iterative quality checks.
- academic-paper-strategist: Systematic strategic planning framework for philosophy and interdisciplinary academic papers targeting preprint platforms (PhilArchive, arXiv, PhilSci-Archive). Use when users want to: (1) plan a paper on a specific topic, (2) identify research gaps and assess originality, (3) develop optimized paper outlines, (4) prepare for preprint submission, or (5) understand platform requirements and writing standards. Triggered by phrases like 'plan a paper on,' 'help me design a paper about,' 'identify research gaps in,' 'is this idea original,' or when users need structured research planning. The skill guides through three phases: Platform Analysis (identifying target venue and studying sample papers), Theoretical Framework (AI-driven literature search and gap identification), and Outline Optimization (structured design with reviewer-perspective self-assessment). Each phase includes quality evaluation standards and validation checkpoints. Output: optimized detailed outline ready for systematic writing (use with academic-paper-composer skill).

- high-end-visual-design: Teaches the AI to design like a high-end agency. Defines the exact fonts, spacing, shadows, card structures, and animations that make a website feel expensive. Blocks all the common defaults that make AI designs look cheap or generic.
- image-to-code: Elite website image-to-code skill for Codex. For visually important web tasks, it must first generate the design image(s) itself, deeply analyze them, then implement the website to match them as closely as possible. In Codex, it must prefer large, readable, section-specific images instead of tiny compressed boards, generate fresh standalone images for sections or detail views instead of cropping old ones, avoid lazy under-generation, avoid cards-inside-cards-inside-cards UI, and keep the hero clean, spacious, readable, and visible on a small laptop.

By default, screens should be shown inside a subtle premium iPhone or similar phone mockup with a visible frame, while the main focus stays on the app content itself. This skill generates images only. It does not write code.

Based on the search results, here's what critics are saying about "AI slop" and homogenized web design in 2026:

## What is AI Slop in Web Design?

AI slop web design refers to generic, mass-produced websites created by AI tools that look identical because they default to the same fonts, colors, and layouts. When you ask an AI design tool for a "modern SaaS landing page," it returns the average of every modern SaaS landing page it has seen—averages that are safe, competent, and completely forgettable.

## The Root Causes

The homogenization stems from compounding defaults in design systems and tools. Tailwind ships with a purple-leaning palette, so a huge share of AI output skews purple. Inter is the default font in nearly every design tool, so everything reads the same. Stack those defaults and you get a homogenized aesthetic that signals one thing to a discerning visitor: nobody made a decision here.

## Real-World Impact

Roughly half of indie SaaS pricing pages launched in 2026 follow the same nine-element template, and the sub-elements inside it cluster just as tightly. Two hundred indie SaaS pages cumulatively form one giant indistinguishable pricing page.

## The Design Critique

AI did not kill design taste—it raised the floor and exposed everyone standing on it. The products that win in 2026 are the ones that use AI to move fast, then spend the saved time making the decisions a model cannot. There are defaults and standards baked into large language models no matter what purpose you use them for. If the user doesn't actively push back against the AI model, then they get the generic output, the lowest common acceptable denominator of aesthetics and taste.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Apple's Liquid Glass design and the criticisms surrounding it:

## Overview

Apple's Liquid Glass was introduced at WWDC 2025 as a translucent, adaptive design language that unifies iOS 26, iPadOS 26, and macOS Tahoe 26 to create a cohesive experience across Apple's ecosystem.

## Legibility and Failure Modes

The primary critique centers on legibility issues. Central to criticisms of Liquid Glass has been OS 26's poor usability – in particular, how the "transparency" of Liquid Glass made everything hard for many users to read. On the iPhone, the very transparent elements looked good on some stock wallpapers but were widely rated unusable on others.

Semi-transparent overlays and low-contrast elements can render text and icons illegible, particularly on intricate backgrounds or in low-light conditions.

## Spatial Interface Context

Industry analysts suggest this move was inspired by the success of VisionOS, which redefined spatial computing, and aims to unify Apple's design language across devices. The "Liquid Glass" UI is an adaptive, physics-based material that solves a critical engineering problem: How do you render white text on an unpredictable background without losing contrast?

## Apple's Response

The first update, two months after the official September 2025 launch, let users disable Liquid Glass's transparency to increase legibility. More recently, Apple has begun testing a setting called 'Tinted' that tones down the gloss and restores a flatter, calmer reading surface.

Based on the search results, I found Kyle Chayka's essay on this topic. Here's what I found:

Chayka wrote about the homogenized websites that Claude Design produces, along with every other AI coding tool. There are defaults and standards baked into large language models no matter what purpose you use them for, and if the user doesn't actively push back against the AI model, they get the generic output, the lowest common acceptable denominator of aesthetics and taste.

This essay is connected to Chayka's broader work on cultural homogenization. His book "Filterworld: How Algorithms Flattened Culture" is an investigation of a world ruled by algorithms, which determine the shape of culture itself. Though digital platforms promise personalization, the net result of so many algorithms is a homogenization of culture.

The essay appears to be part of Chayka's ongoing exploration of how technology flattens and homogenizes culture across different domains, from interior design (his earlier "Welcome to Airspace" essay) to now AI-generated web design.

content.content:
# Web Design Movements & Shipping Reality

## Named Visual Styles/Trends

**Actually Shipping:**
- Bento grid layouts (now default across major tech companies)
- Dark mode as primary theme
- Design systems with token-based architecture
- AI readability layers (schema markup, llms.txt, agents.json)
- Anti-grid brutalism (counter-movement to polish)

**Demo-Only/Overpromised:**
- Kinetic typography: "almost never ships in production" because it "fights screen readers, fights search crawlers"
- Glassmorphism 2.0: survived but "in a more restrained form," causing 15-30% FPS drops on mid-tier Android devices
- Organic blob shapes: "almost never ship on B2B SaaS, e-commerce or any conversion-critical flow"
- WebGL/3D: restricted to "when the brand is the experience (creative agencies, fashion houses, art portfolios)"

## Critique of Generic/Templated Design

The author warns against template convergence, noting that "when everyone else looks like Apple, looking different becomes the differentiator." The brutalism counter-trend emerged specifically as positioning against ubiquitous bento adoption.

Sustainability and AI personalization are flagged as trends that sound compelling but face adoption barriers (cost-optimization priorities, GDPR restrictions respectively).

Based on the search results, here's what's happening with the personal website revival and small web movement in 2026:

## The Personal Website Renaissance

In 2026, tech enthusiasts like Alan W. Smith are leading a renaissance of personal websites, shifting from algorithm-driven social media due to privacy concerns and content control issues. Alan W. Smith declared 2026 as "The Year of My Website," signaling a broader shift away from centralized social media toward decentralized, self-owned digital spaces.

## Anti-Corporate and Indie Web Movement

The "Indie Web" movement is a DIY-rooted answer to the larger, corporatized Web. The indie web is built on a foundation of curation and human intention. Before social media, websites were the norm. You would find a site, share a site, add it to your bookmarks and that site would link you to other sites. This is where we got the concept of "browsing the web."

## Distinctiveness Against Templates

The 2026 design trends reflect a push toward handmade, distinctive aesthetics. Y2K design feels authentic, anti-corporate, and playfully irreverent. Anti-corporate design works best for fashion, lifestyle, culture, and creative studios, with brands using it to look bold, creative, and culturally aware rather than overly corporate.

## Why This Matters

The experience of checking an RSS reader feels qualitatively different from scrolling social media—more intentional, less addictive, more respectful of attention and time. For creators, RSS subscribers represent highly engaged audience members who chose deliberately to follow their work.

input.prompt: What named techniques, aesthetics or movements does this year-in-review identify as dominant in 2025 web/creative development? List concrete named things.

content.content:
# Named Techniques and Aesthetics Dominant in 2025 Web Development

Based on Codrops' year-in-review, these concrete techniques and movements shaped creative development in 2025:

## 3D & WebGL Technologies
- **Three.js** - dominant framework for 3D scenes
- **React Three Fiber** - 3D within React ecosystems
- **WebGPU** - emerging GPU computing standard
- **TSL (Three.js Shading Language)** - shader development approach

## Animation & Motion Systems
- **GSAP** - animation library (became fully free in 2025)
- **SplitText** and **MorphSVG** plugins - text and shape animation
- **Scroll-triggered animations** - scroll-driven interactions
- **Framer Motion** - React animation framework
- **Rive** - vector animation tool with data binding

## UI/Interaction Patterns
- **Carousels** (infinite, 3D, wavy variants)
- **Particle systems** and generative effects
- **Draggable elements** and interactive grids
- **Scroll-smoother effects** and parallax techniques
- **Dithering shaders** - retro aesthetic technique

## Design-to-Code Workflows
- **Webflow integration** with 3D and animation
- **Figma-to-WordPress** pipelines (via Droip)
- **Blender-to-web** 3D asset pipelines

## Emerging Areas
- **AI agents** for performance monitoring
- **WebXR** immersive experiences
- **Procedural generation** - generative art techniques

results.title: The generic style of AI web design — Kyle Chayka Industries
results.snippet: The single strongest primary source for the pipeline's anti-template core rule. Chayka (author of Filterworld, on cultural homogenization / 'AirSpace') names the AI-default web look as a legible style in its own right: LLM coding tools ship baked-in defaults, and absent active pushback the user receives 'the lowest common acceptable denominator of aesthetics and taste.' Names Claude Design specifically. This is design-press critique by a named critic rather than an agency listicle, and it supplies the framing sentence for a 'what to avoid' section: the generic look is not an absence of style, it is a style with a name and a source. Supports the anti-template rule directly; no conflict with any budget or a11y constraint.

results.title: Web Design Trends 2026: What Actually Held Up After Six Months — Studio Meyer
results.snippet: Rare trend piece structured almost exactly like the repo's four-part STYLES.md shape: each named movement gets a shipping verdict and a failure mode. Separates what actually ships (bento grid — now so default across major tech companies that it IS the cliché; dark-mode-primary; token-based systems; anti-grid brutalism as deliberate counter-positioning) from demo-only looks (kinetic typography 'almost never ships in production' because it 'fights screen readers, fights search crawlers'; organic blob shapes 'almost never ship on conversion-critical flows'; WebGL restricted to 'when the brand IS the experience'). Gives a measured-ish cost number for Glassmorphism 2.0 (15-30% FPS drop on mid-tier Android) — flag as vendor-measured, not peer-reviewed. Money quote for the anti-template rule: 'when everyone else looks like Apple, looking different becomes the differentiator.' Directly usable as new STYLES.md 'Fails' clauses and as a cliché blocklist (bento grid, blobs, kinetic type).

results.title: 2025: A Very Special Year in Review — Codrops
results.snippet: The named practitioner-source the angle brief asked for, and the best inventory of what the creative-dev community actually built in 2025 across 51 published tutorials. Concrete technique names to cross-check against the existing 72: WebGPU and TSL (Three.js Shading Language), dithering shaders as a retro-aesthetic technique, procedural generation, particle systems, infinite/3D/wavy carousels, draggable interactive grids, scroll-smoother and parallax, Rive vector animation with data binding, GSAP going fully free in 2025 (with SplitText and MorphSVG now unpaywalled — a real change to what a self-hosted, vendored pipeline can legally ship). Caveat for the deliverable: Codrops indexes demos, not production sites, so pair every entry here with the Studio Meyer shipping verdict before promoting it to a style; most of these violate the sub-100KB shell and belong strictly in the deferred heavy layer.

results.title: Meet Liquid Glass — WWDC25, Apple Developer
results.snippet: Primary source (platform HIG-tier, not commentary) for the single biggest named movement of 2025-2026 that the existing 32-style list does not cover. Defines Liquid Glass as an adaptive physics-based *material* rather than a decoration — mechanics are lensing/refraction of what is behind the surface, specular highlight response to motion, and adaptive tinting to hold contrast over unpredictable backdrops. Important distinction for a STYLES.md entry: this is the successor to, and explicitly not, the flat blur-and-transparency glassmorphism the pipeline may already document. 'Right when' condition per Apple: a floating control layer above content, never the content layer itself.

results.title: Getting Clarity on Apple's Liquid Glass — CSS-Tricks
results.snippet: The web-implementability half of the Liquid Glass entry, and the reason it survives the pipeline's constraints. Works through what CSS can and cannot natively do here — backdrop-filter gets the blur but not the refraction/lensing, which needs SVG filters (feDisplacementMap/feTurbulence) or a shader, i.e. a real fork between a cheap CSS/SVG-native tier and a heavy runtime tier. Pair with the documented failure mode from the same news cycle: Apple shipped a Reduce Transparency escape hatch and then a 'Tinted' setting in iOS 26.1 after legibility backlash — semi-transparent overlays go illegible over busy or low-light backdrops. That is a WCAG-contrast violation waiting to happen, so any Liquid Glass style entry must ship the tinted/opaque variant as its designed reduced state, not as an afterthought.

results.title: Craft — Rauno Freiberg
results.snippet: The named practitioner reference from the brief (Freiberg, design engineer at Vercel, author of cmdk). A running collection of short notes on the small decisions that make an interface feel deliberate rather than assembled — the companion essay 'Invisible Details of Interaction Design' (rauno.me/craft/interaction-design) is the canonical practitioner text on why some interactions feel right. Relevance is medium for Area 3 specifically (it names no aesthetic movement) but high for the pipeline's underlying thesis and for Areas 4-5: it argues distinctiveness comes from accumulated micro-decisions, not from picking a different style label — which is the strongest available counter-argument to a style-catalogue approach and worth quoting as a caveat in the report. Companion source in the same circle: Emil Kowalski's interfacecraft.dev (40+ articles, Linear design engineer).
